newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak central bank waits to vet M2 steps - paper.
newsitem.headline: Slovak central bank waits to vet M2 steps - paper.

text.p: The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) is still waiting to review the effects of its recent measures to stem a growing money supply, the economic daily Hospodarske Noviny reported on Wednesday.
"We expect the first reliable results (of the measures) in October-November, or by the end of the year," Elena Kohutikova, head of NBS Monetary Division, told the paper in an interview.

In mid-July, the NBS approved a series of measures aimed at stemming the country's burgeoning money supply, including raising bank's minimum reserve levels, a key lending rate and widening the band in which it fixes the crown to scare off speculative hot money.

"To now, we cannot unambiguously judge whether the measures' primary goal to regulate an over-dynamic increase in credits to the economy, which are causing an unproportional trade balance deficit, will be fulfilled," Kohutikova said.
The trade deficit for the first seven months of the year widened to 31.9 billion crowns, from 26.97 billion for the January-June period, boosted mainly by surging imports.

"Our (currently) slighter moves within the band, which we are of course ready to intensify, should be efficient enough," Kohutikova said. "A possible loss on an exchange rate change is relatively high."
The NBS fixes the crown daily against a 60/40 percent mark/dollar basket within plus/minus five percent of the basket's midpoint.
But she added: "We believe that we will succeed to create a sufficient rate of uncertainty for such (speculative) capital and prevent it from its significant inflow".
So far, she said there have been "no significant signs of an overflowing" speculative capital.
"The NBS wants to continue creating a stable exchange rate also to allow businesses to calculate in a long term within the restructuring process," Kohutikova said.

But she added: "We warn that a negative affect on the balance of payments could occur in the future if restructuring is not intesified, and loans which have entered the economy ... are not used to secure our enterprises' participation abroad".

She said that of total imports to Slovakia in the first half of the year, some 50 percent were investment imports, but a third of them were technologies, a third cars, while the remainder could not be identified.
"We warn that if such tendencies in imports continue longer, they could have a negative impact on the quality and competivenesss of our exports in the future," she said.
